title: Adolescent Development
tagline: Understanding the storm, the struggle, and the strength of adolescence.
welcome: Adolescence is not a problem to be managed; it is a passage to be honored. This course teaches you to walk beside young people through one of life's most intense transformations.
vignette: A fifteen-year-old who once loved debate now answers every question with a shrug. His grades slide, his friends change, his phone never sleeps. His father calls it rebellion. His counselor suspects a story underneath, and wonders which lens will reveal it.
vignette_attr: A secondary-school referral, drawn from supervised practice
description: An in-depth study of adolescent physical, cognitive, moral, and identity development. The course examines puberty and body image, formal and postformal thought, moral reasoning, identity and self-esteem, peer culture and the digital world, risk and resilience, and faith formation, preparing counselors to meet adolescents with developmental empathy rather than adult anxiety.
questions: What is the adolescent actually trying to become?
How much of this behavior is stage, and how much is signal?
How do we hold authority and alliance at the same time?
importance: Adolescents are reached through respect for their emerging identity, not through control
Most adult mental health stories begin in adolescence; early skilled support changes them
The digital world has rewritten adolescent social life; counselors must be literate in it
cases: the fifteen-year-old whose shrug replaced a once-vivid voice
a thirteen-year-old whose online life is brilliant and whose offline life is fading
a seventeen-year-old standing at the edge of decisions that will echo for decades
misconceptions: that adolescent turmoil is abnormal, when a degree of storm is a normative part of individuation
that adolescents cannot engage in deep counseling, when they often engage more honestly than adults
figures: who named identity versus role confusion as the adolescent task
whose formal operations open the door to abstract and moral thought
who traced the development of moral reasoning through adolescence
outcomes: You will describe physical, cognitive, moral, and identity development in adolescence.
Apply identity and moral development theories
You will use Erikson, Marcia, and Kohlberg to understand real adolescents.
You will weigh risk and resilience with structured, developmentally attuned tools.
You will build alliance that honors autonomy while providing steady authority.
You will shape interventions that fit the adolescent's stage and culture.
You will assess how social media and screens shape identity and mood.
modules: Historical and cultural views of adolescence
A clear definition frees you from both panic and dismissal.
Puberty, Body Image, and Physical Change
The timing and tempo of puberty
Puberty reshapes the self before the mind has words for it; counselors supply the words.
Adolescent egocentrism and the personal fable
Understanding adolescent logic prevents us from misreading it as defiance.
Identity work is the central task; every intervention either aids or interrupts it.
Peers, Culture, and the Digital World
Social media and the curated self
The peer and digital worlds are the adolescent's first society; we must know their rules.
Risk, Resilience, and Positive Youth Development
We count strengths as carefully as risks, because strengths are what we build on.
Confidentiality and its limits with minors
The relationship is the intervention; this module builds it deliberately.
practicum: Practice centers on alliance and assessment with real adolescent dynamics.
Adolescent interview practice with structured feedback
assessment: Assessment tests both knowledge and relational skill.
A developmental interview recording with reflection
tips: Interview one adolescent this semester and listen more than you speak
Track one digital-cultural trend each week and note its emotional payload
Practice holding both authority and warmth in the same sentence
integration: This course grounds every adolescent-facing course that follows, from crisis intervention to substance abuse counseling. You cannot intervene well where you have not first understood.
faith: Adolescence is often when faith becomes personal or is set aside. We approach that searching with reverence, walking with young people as they ask ultimate questions for themselves.
closing: May you meet adolescents not as problems but as pilgrims, and may your presence make their passage safer.
